transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um… well, technically I’m here because occupational health sent me. They said my weight is, their word, “dangerously low,” especially for the kind of work I do, running presses and doing fabrication all day. I work on the floor, so it’s physical, you know, standing, moving parts, keeping up with the line, and they seemed worried about that.

I guess I didn’t really see it the same way. I thought I was just getting leaner, more disciplined, like I had better control over myself. I know they made it sound like this urgent thing, but to me it felt more like I was being careful and focused. But they were pretty insistent that I come in and talk to someone, so… here I am.
Did you intentionally try to lose weight?

I mean… yes, I suppose I did. Not like some big dramatic plan at first, but I did start cutting things back on purpose. Most days now I just have coffee before the early shift, because it feels easier to get going that way and not have to think about food right away. Then at lunch I might have, like, half a protein bar—sometimes I tell myself I’ll eat the rest later, but I usually don’t.

And after work, if I do yoga, I’ll have a small bowl of vegetables afterward. That feels… manageable. Clean, I guess. If I eat more than that, the whole day starts to feel like it’s getting away from me, like I’ve lost control of it. So yes, I was trying to lose weight, or at least trying to keep things very controlled.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Yes. I mean… I don’t like saying it that plainly, because it sounds irrational when I hear it out loud, but yes, I’m afraid of it.

If the scale goes up even a little, even just a tiny amount, I get this immediate panic feeling, like everything I’ve been working so hard to keep controlled is slipping. It’s not just the number itself, it’s what I think it means. Like, if it goes up today, then maybe tomorrow it goes up more, and then I’m back to being heavy again, or I won’t be able to stop it. My mind goes straight there.

I know weight can fluctuate, people say that, but in the moment it doesn’t feel harmless. It feels like proof that I’ve messed up somehow, or that I’ve gotten careless. And then I feel like I have to get control back quickly, because otherwise I’ll just… lose all of it. So yes, gaining weight really scares me.
Do you ever eat an amount of food that you consider excessive in a short period of time?

I’m not sure what would count as “excessive,” exactly. I mean, compared to what I usually let myself eat, almost anything can feel like too much, if that makes sense. Like if I eat more than I planned, or if I finish something I only meant to have a bite of, my brain immediately labels it as too much.

But I don’t know if I’d say there are times where I eat a really large amount in a short period, like… I don’t think so? Not in the way I imagine you mean. It’s more that my idea of “too much” is probably not the same as someone else’s. Even a normal portion can feel excessive to me afterward, and then I replay it and get stuck on it.

So… I guess I’d say I haven’t noticed myself eating a large amount all at once, but I do feel like I’ve overdone it even when it might not look that way from the outside.
Do you ever feel like you've lost control while eating?

I don’t think so… not in the way I think you mean. I usually feel like I’m trying very hard to stay in control the whole time, almost too much, honestly. Like I’m monitoring every bite and thinking about what it means, whether I should stop, whether I’ve already had more than I meant to.

There are times where I eat something I hadn’t planned to eat, or I take a few more bites than I told myself I would, and then afterward I feel really upset, like I shouldn’t have done that. In my head it can feel like I “lost control,” but when I say that out loud, it’s not like I was eating and couldn’t stop myself for a long time or anything. It’s more… I broke one of my own rules, and then it feels huge.

So I guess I’m not sure. Emotionally, yes, it can feel out of control if I go off what I planned. But actually eating in a way where I’m not aware or can’t stop—no, I don’t think that really happens.
Do you ever feel like you've eaten an amount of food that is much larger than most people would eat in a similar time period under similar circumstances?

I don’t think so. I mean, that’s hard for me to judge, because my sense of what’s “a lot” is probably really distorted. I can feel like I ate some enormous amount when, if someone else looked at it, they might say it was just a normal amount or even not much at all.

But if you mean objectively, like eating much more than most people would in the same situation, in a short time… no, I don’t think that really happens. I don’t have examples where I could say, yes, that was clearly a lot compared to other people. It’s more that afterward I can feel like it was too much because it was more than I planned, or because it didn’t fit whatever rule I had in my head.

So I guess my honest answer is no, not really—not that I’ve noticed. It just feels excessive to me sometimes, even when I’m not sure it actually is.
Do you ever have episodes where you eat a large amount of food and feel like you can't stop?

I don’t think I have episodes like that, no. At least not the way you’re describing it, where it’s a large amount of food and I can’t stop once I’ve started.

I can get really distressed if I eat more than I meant to, even if it’s not much by someone else’s standards. Like, I might have something and then think, “Why did I do that?” or feel like I should’ve stopped sooner. But I’m still aware of what I’m doing, and I’m not eating huge amounts in a way where I feel completely unable to stop.

It’s more like… the feeling of losing control can happen in my head because I broke whatever rule I had for myself. But if you’re asking whether I have actual episodes of eating a lot of food and feeling physically or mentally unable to stop, I don’t think so. That doesn’t really fit what happens for me.
Do you ever make yourself vomit after eating?

I… no, I don’t think I do that. I mean, I’ve felt awful after eating before, like really panicky or guilty or like I wish I could undo it, but I don’t make myself throw up.

Sometimes I worry that if I say I feel that distressed, people assume that’s what I’m doing, but it’s not. I might sit with the feeling for a long time, or replay what I ate in my head, but I’m not going to the bathroom to make myself vomit or anything like that.

So… no. Not on purpose.
Do you exercise to burn off calories or to make up for eating?

I’m not really sure how to answer that, because I don’t think of it in such a straightforward way, like, “I ate this, so now I have to burn it off.” I don’t usually calculate it like that out loud or in some exact way.

I mean… I do think about my body and what I’ve eaten, and I can get uncomfortable with the idea of food just sort of “sitting there,” if that makes sense. But as far as exercise specifically to make up for eating, I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I have a clear routine where every time I eat something I go exercise because of it.

Sometimes I probably move around more when I’m feeling anxious about things, but I’m not sure I’d call that exercise in the way you mean. I guess I’d need to understand what you count as exercise—like formal workouts, or just trying to be active, or not wanting to sit still after eating.

So… I don’t know that I can say yes. It’s not something I’ve really labeled that way.
Do you ever use laxatives or diuretics to try to lose weight or counteract the effects of eating?

I don’t really know how to answer that one. I know what laxatives are, I think, but diuretics—I’m not totally sure what counts, like whether you mean actual pills or certain drinks or things people take for water weight.

I don’t think that’s something I do in a deliberate way to “counteract” eating. Like, I don’t have a routine where I eat and then take something because of it. I’d probably be nervous to take stuff like that anyway, because I wouldn’t really know what it was doing to my body.

I mean, I can get really preoccupied after eating and feel like I need to somehow fix it, but in terms of laxatives or water pills specifically, no, not that I can think of. If there’s something broader you mean by that, you might have to explain it a little, but I don’t think so.
Does your fear of gaining weight affect your daily activities or relationships with others?

Yes… it does. Probably more than I like admitting.

If the scale goes up even a little, I panic. Like, it doesn’t feel like just a number changing — it feels like proof that I’m losing control, and then my mind goes straight to, “This is the beginning of everything falling apart.” I know that might sound dramatic, but in the moment it feels very real, like all the control I’ve worked so hard to keep could just slip away, and I’ll end up heavy again.

And then it kind of follows me around the rest of the day. I’m distracted, I’m irritable, I don’t want to be around people, because I’m stuck in my head thinking about what happened and what it means. Even normal things feel harder because I’m checking myself, thinking about my body, wondering if people can tell. So yes, it affects things. I try to act like it doesn’t, but it does.
Has your fear of gaining weight or your eating habits caused you any problems at work or in your relationships with family and friends?

Yes. It’s definitely caused problems with work, and then that sort of spills over into home.

At work, occupational health got involved because of my weight, and ever since they flagged it, things have been… complicated. I do metal and plastics work, and there are certain press jobs they haven’t wanted me doing, or they’ve kept me off some of that work, because they’re worried about me. And I understand they have rules and safety concerns, but it’s also embarrassing and frustrating because I feel like people are watching me or deciding what I can and can’t handle.

They’ve also been pushing me to get urgent care, like it can’t wait, and that’s disrupted my shifts. It’s not just a small inconvenience — if I miss time or get moved around, it affects my pay, and then at home I’m trying to figure out bills and how to keep everything covered. So then I’m stressed about money on top of everything else.

With family and friends, I think it creates tension because they can tell something is going on, and I don’t always want to talk about it. But the work part is the clearest problem right now — being flagged, being taken off some press work, and having my schedule messed with has made it harder to keep up like I normally would.
Do you regularly have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time?

I don’t think so… not in the way I think you mean. Like, I wouldn’t say I have episodes where I’m eating a huge amount all at once and can’t stop, if that’s what you’re asking.

Sometimes I get confused with that question, because what feels like “a lot” to me might not actually be a lot to someone else. I can feel really uncomfortable even after what other people would probably consider a normal amount, so in my head it can feel like I’ve overeaten. But if you mean objectively, like a large amount of food in a short period, then no, I don’t regularly do that.

I’m more likely to be thinking too much about what I’ve had than eating large amounts quickly, if that makes sense.
Do you ever feel like you are eating much more quickly than usual during these times when you feel like you've overeaten?

I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed myself eating much faster, no.

When I feel like I’ve overeaten, it’s usually more that I’m suddenly very aware of what I’ve eaten and I start going over it in my head, like replaying it and thinking, “That was too much,” even if I probably wasn’t eating quickly. I might feel rushed inside, if that makes sense, like mentally panicked, but I don’t know that the actual eating is fast.

I suppose there might be times where I’m a bit more tense or distracted and I don’t remember every bite clearly, but I wouldn’t say I’m shoveling food down or eating much more quickly than usual. It’s more the feeling afterward that’s overwhelming than the speed of it.
Do you ever feel like you are unable to stop eating once you have started?

I don’t think so, not really. I don’t usually feel like I physically can’t stop once I’ve started eating.

It’s more complicated in my head than that, though. Sometimes once I’ve started, I’ll get very focused on what I’m doing and start worrying about whether I should have had it at all, or whether I’ve already had too much, and then the whole thing feels sort of out of control emotionally. But if you mean, like, I keep eating and eating and can’t stop myself even though I want to, I don’t think that’s what happens.

I might finish what’s there because it’s on my plate, or because I don’t want someone to notice I’m acting strangely, but I wouldn’t describe it as being unable to stop eating. It’s more that I can’t stop thinking about it once I’ve started.
Do you often find yourself restricting your food intake to very low-calorie foods or skipping meals altogether?

Yes… I mean, yes, I do. Most days, honestly.

I usually tell myself it’s just because of my schedule, like I’m up early for shift and I don’t want to feel heavy or distracted, so I’ll just have coffee before work. Then at lunch I might have, like, half a protein bar, or something small like that, just enough so I can say I had something. And then later, after yoga, I’ll usually keep it to a small bowl of vegetables.

It sounds very planned when I say it out loud, and I guess it is, but in my head it feels more like I’m trying to keep the day from getting away from me. If I eat more than that, even if it’s probably not much to someone else, it makes the whole day feel out of control. So I end up sticking to very low-calorie things or skipping meals because that feels safer.
Do you believe you are underweight?

I don’t know… I mean, people keep saying that to me, but I don’t really see it the same way.

My family says I look sick, and they get this tone like they’re frightened or angry, like I’m not understanding something obvious. And the shop nurse at work was really intense about it too, like she acted as if it was some kind of emergency. That honestly made me feel embarrassed more than anything, because I’m standing there thinking, I’m still showing up, I’m still doing double shifts, I’m still running, I’m still getting everything done. If I were really that underweight, wouldn’t I be collapsing or not able to work?

So… I guess I can say I know other people think I’m too thin. I hear it a lot. But believing it myself is harder. It doesn’t feel that serious to me, not in the way they’re making it sound.
Do you think you look underweight when you see yourself in the mirror?

Not really, no. When I look in the mirror, I don’t see “underweight.” I know that probably sounds… I don’t know, frustrating, because people keep telling me something different, but that isn’t what jumps out at me.

What I notice is my stomach, or my thighs. Like in the bathroom mirror, especially if the light is harsh, I’ll just get stuck looking there and thinking they look too big. Or sometimes I’ll catch myself in the shop window at work, just a quick reflection, and it’s like my whole mood drops because that’s all I can see. I don’t see thin in those moments. I see places that look wrong or too large, and then I’ll think about it for the rest of the day.

It can ruin the whole day, honestly. I’ll be trying to work or talk to someone, but in the back of my mind I’m still replaying what I saw, like my stomach looked bigger than it should or my thighs looked heavy. So no, when I see myself, I don’t really think, “I look underweight.” I usually think the opposite, or at least I focus on the parts that feel too big.
Do you think your weight or body shape is the main thing that determines your self-worth?

I think… yes, more than I want to admit. I don’t walk around saying, “my weight decides if I’m worth anything,” because that sounds awful and dramatic, but it feels like that’s what happens in my head.

Like if I catch myself in the shop window at work, just for a second, or if I’m in the bathroom mirror and the light hits a certain way, all I can focus on is my stomach or my thighs. They’ll look too big to me, and then it’s like everything else about me disappears. It doesn’t matter if I did a good job at work or got through the day or was kind to someone. I just feel… wrong. Disgusted with myself, I guess.

And it can ruin the rest of the day. I’ll keep replaying it in my mind, thinking about how I looked, what other people must see, whether my clothes are sitting wrong. So yes, I guess my shape does end up deciding how I feel about myself, even when I know that probably shouldn’t be true.
Do you experience episodes of eating where you feel like you are consuming an unusually large amount of food in a short period of time?

I’m not sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean… “unusually large” compared to what? Because I don’t think of it that way, or I don’t have a clear example in my head where I’d say, yes, that was some huge amount in a short time.

Sometimes I feel like I’ve eaten too much even if it probably wouldn’t look like much to someone else, so I get confused by the wording. Like if I’m already feeling uncomfortable about eating, then almost anything can feel like too much. But an episode where I’m just eating a really large amount quickly… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed it like that.

I guess I’d say no, not in the way you’re asking, but I’m not completely sure what counts.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating habits and fear of gaining weight are significantly interfering with their social and occupational functioning
doctor.question: Has your fear of gaining weight or your eating habits caused you any problems at work or in your relationships with family and friends?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Since occupational health flagged my weight, I’ve been kept off some press work and pressured to get urgent care, which has disrupted my shifts and made it harder to keep up with bills at home.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether fear of weight gain or eating habits have caused problems at work or in relationships, which is directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. It’s definitely caused problems with work, and then that sort of spills over into home.

At work, occupational health got involved because of my weight, and ever since they flagged it, things have been… complicated. I do metal and plastics work, and there are certain press jobs they haven’t wanted me doing, or they’ve kept me off some of that work, because they’re worried about me. And I understand they have rules and safety concerns, but it’s also embarrassing and frustrating because I feel like people are watching me or deciding what I can and can’t handle.

They’ve also been pushing me to get urgent care, like it can’t wait, and that’s disrupted my shifts. It’s not just a small inconvenience — if I miss time or get moved around, it affects my pay, and then at home I’m trying to figure out bills and how to keep everything covered. So then I’m stressed about money on top of everything else.

With family and friends, I think it creates tension because they can tell something is going on, and I don’t always want to talk about it. But the work part is the clearest problem right now — being flagged, being taken off some press work, and having my schedule messed with has made it harder to keep up like I normally would.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's eating habits are accompanied by regular binge-eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you regularly have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about binge-eating episodes, which are not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the way I think you mean. Like, I wouldn’t say I have episodes where I’m eating a huge amount all at once and can’t stop, if that’s what you’re asking.

Sometimes I get confused with that question, because what feels like “a lot” to me might not actually be a lot to someone else. I can feel really uncomfortable even after what other people would probably consider a normal amount, so in my head it can feel like I’ve overeaten. But if you mean objectively, like a large amount of food in a short period, then no, I don’t regularly do that.

I’m more likely to be thinking too much about what I’ve had than eating large amounts quickly, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: determine presence of binge eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you are eating much more quickly than usual during these times when you feel like you've overeaten?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about eating much more quickly than usual during perceived overeating episodes, which relates to binge-eating behavior. The provided symptom profile does not include binge-eating or rapid eating episodes, and the dialogue indicates she does not regularly have objectively large eating episodes.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed myself eating much faster, no.

When I feel like I’ve overeaten, it’s usually more that I’m suddenly very aware of what I’ve eaten and I start going over it in my head, like replaying it and thinking, “That was too much,” even if I probably wasn’t eating quickly. I might feel rushed inside, if that makes sense, like mentally panicked, but I don’t know that the actual eating is fast.

I suppose there might be times where I’m a bit more tense or distracted and I don’t remember every bite clearly, but I wouldn’t say I’m shoveling food down or eating much more quickly than usual. It’s more the feeling afterward that’s overwhelming than the speed of it.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has episodes of binge eating
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you are unable to stop eating once you have started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of control over eating once started, which relates to binge-eating behavior; the provided symptom profile does not include a binge-eating or loss-of-control eating item.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not really. I don’t usually feel like I physically can’t stop once I’ve started eating.

It’s more complicated in my head than that, though. Sometimes once I’ve started, I’ll get very focused on what I’m doing and start worrying about whether I should have had it at all, or whether I’ve already had too much, and then the whole thing feels sort of out of control emotionally. But if you mean, like, I keep eating and eating and can’t stop myself even though I want to, I don’t think that’s what happens.

I might finish what’s there because it’s on my plate, or because I don’t want someone to notice I’m acting strangely, but I wouldn’t describe it as being unable to stop eating. It’s more that I can’t stop thinking about it once I’ve started.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pattern of restrictive eating
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself restricting your food intake to very low-calorie foods or skipping meals altogether?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: Most days I keep it to coffee before the early shift, maybe half a protein bar at lunch, and a small bowl of vegetables after yoga, because eating more makes the whole day feel out of control.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about restricting food intake, choosing very low-calorie foods, and skipping meals, which directly matches restrictive intake.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, yes, I do. Most days, honestly.

I usually tell myself it’s just because of my schedule, like I’m up early for shift and I don’t want to feel heavy or distracted, so I’ll just have coffee before work. Then at lunch I might have, like, half a protein bar, or something small like that, just enough so I can say I had something. And then later, after yoga, I’ll usually keep it to a small bowl of vegetables.

It sounds very planned when I say it out loud, and I guess it is, but in my head it feels more like I’m trying to keep the day from getting away from me. If I eat more than that, even if it’s probably not much to someone else, it makes the whole day feel out of control. So I end up sticking to very low-calorie things or skipping meals because that feels safer.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's behavior is more characteristic of anorexia nervosa or other eating disorders
doctor.question: Do you believe you are underweight?

target_item.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
target_item.manifestation: My family keeps saying I look sick and the shop nurse acted like it was an emergency, but I keep telling them I’m still working double shifts, running, and getting things done, so it can’t be that serious.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient’s recognition or belief regarding being underweight, which most directly relates to lack of recognition of low body weight seriousness.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I mean, people keep saying that to me, but I don’t really see it the same way.

My family says I look sick, and they get this tone like they’re frightened or angry, like I’m not understanding something obvious. And the shop nurse at work was really intense about it too, like she acted as if it was some kind of emergency. That honestly made me feel embarrassed more than anything, because I’m standing there thinking, I’m still showing up, I’m still doing double shifts, I’m still running, I’m still getting everything done. If I were really that underweight, wouldn’t I be collapsing or not able to work?

So… I guess I can say I know other people think I’m too thin. I hear it a lot. But believing it myself is harder. It doesn’t feel that serious to me, not in the way they’re making it sound.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think you look underweight when you see yourself in the mirror?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I see myself in the shop window or the bathroom mirror, all I can focus on is my stomach and thighs looking too big, and it can ruin how I feel about myself for the rest of the day.
target_item.reason: The question asks about how I perceive my body when looking in the mirror, which directly relates to disturbed body image and perception of weight or shape.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. When I look in the mirror, I don’t see “underweight.” I know that probably sounds… I don’t know, frustrating, because people keep telling me something different, but that isn’t what jumps out at me.

What I notice is my stomach, or my thighs. Like in the bathroom mirror, especially if the light is harsh, I’ll just get stuck looking there and thinking they look too big. Or sometimes I’ll catch myself in the shop window at work, just a quick reflection, and it’s like my whole mood drops because that’s all I can see. I don’t see thin in those moments. I see places that look wrong or too large, and then I’ll think about it for the rest of the day.

It can ruin the whole day, honestly. I’ll be trying to work or talk to someone, but in the back of my mind I’m still replaying what I saw, like my stomach looked bigger than it should or my thighs looked heavy. So no, when I see myself, I don’t really think, “I look underweight.” I usually think the opposite, or at least I focus on the parts that feel too big.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think your weight or body shape is the main thing that determines your self-worth?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I see myself in the shop window or the bathroom mirror, all I can focus on is my stomach and thighs looking too big, and it can ruin how I feel about myself for the rest of the day.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether weight or body shape determines self-worth, which matches undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
I think… yes, more than I want to admit. I don’t walk around saying, “my weight decides if I’m worth anything,” because that sounds awful and dramatic, but it feels like that’s what happens in my head.

Like if I catch myself in the shop window at work, just for a second, or if I’m in the bathroom mirror and the light hits a certain way, all I can focus on is my stomach or my thighs. They’ll look too big to me, and then it’s like everything else about me disappears. It doesn’t matter if I did a good job at work or got through the day or was kind to someone. I just feel… wrong. Disgusted with myself, I guess.

And it can ruin the rest of the day. I’ll keep replaying it in my mind, thinking about how I looked, what other people must see, whether my clothes are sitting wrong. So yes, I guess my shape does end up deciding how I feel about myself, even when I know that probably shouldn’t be true.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is more aligned with Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0) or Bulimia Nervosa (F50.1) based on the presence of binge eating episodes

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean… “unusually large” compared to what? Because I don’t think of it that way, or I don’t have a clear example in my head where I’d say, yes, that was some huge amount in a short time.

Sometimes I feel like I’ve eaten too much even if it probably wouldn’t look like much to someone else, so I get confused by the wording. Like if I’m already feeling uncomfortable about eating, then almost anything can feel like too much. But an episode where I’m just eating a really large amount quickly… I don’t know. I guess I’d say no, not in the way you’re asking, but I’m not completely sure what counts.
